blocks.text: Replace many-to-many references between objects with one object that owns their interaction.

Colleagues no longer know each other. They talk to a **mediator**, which decides who hears what and in which order. Coupling moves from a web of N-to-N links into a single class, which makes the colleagues reusable and the interaction rules easy to find and change.

items: **Trade:** simpler colleagues, a more complex mediator.

blocks.text: A mediator accumulates logic by design. Watch it: unchecked, it turns into a god class.

cards.expectedOutput:
ana=[cy: hello]
bo=[ana: hi, cy: hello]
cy=[ana: hi]

walkthrough.note: The mediator interface is all colleagues ever see. It offers only the coordination operations they need.
A colleague keeps a reference to the room, never to other members. It sends through the mediator and just records what it receives.
The concrete mediator owns the rules: broadcast to everyone but the sender, and drop messages from muted members. Policy lives here alone.
Wiring: each member enters the room, which registers it. Members are created independently of each other.
Muting `bo` changes behavior without touching any `Member`. The room drops `spam`, so no one receives it.

blocks.text: Fields of a checkout form that depend on each other.

Choosing a country enables a state dropdown, changes the postal-code validator, hides VAT fields and recalculates shipping. Wiring each widget to the others yields dozens of cross-references. A `CheckoutFormMediator` receives change events from widgets and updates the rest. Widgets stay dumb and reusable; every rule about field dependencies reads top to bottom in one class.
Payoff: adding a field rule edits one class, and widgets are testable and reusable on other forms.

lists.title: Use when
items: Objects reference each other in a tangle that is hard to follow.
Interaction rules change more often than the objects themselves.
You want colleagues reusable in other contexts.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: Two objects interact in one simple way: a direct call is clearer.
The interaction is pure notification; Observer is lighter.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: The mediator becomes a god class holding all business logic.
Colleagues sneak references to each other, bypassing the mediator.
The mediator is a single point of change and a testing hotspot.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: An in-process event bus or Spring's `ApplicationEventPublisher` acts as a mediator for decoupled components.
For UI state, a single state holder with reducers plays the mediator's role.

rows.difference: Observer is one-to-many notification with the subject unaware of listeners' logic. A mediator is many-to-many coordination that contains the rules. A mediator is often built on observers.
A facade simplifies access to a subsystem in one direction and the subsystem does not know it. A mediator is two-way: the colleagues know it and depend on it.
Colleagues often send commands or events to the mediator, which dispatches them to the right collaborators.
A chain passes one request through handlers that do not know each other. A mediator knows every participant and routes freely among them.
A controller in MVC mediates between the view and the model, so they stay unaware of each other.

entries.name: javax.swing.ButtonGroup
entries.detail: Radio buttons never reference each other; selecting one notifies the group, which deselects the previously selected button.

entries.name: EventBus
entries.detail: Posters and subscribers share only the bus, which routes each event to the `@Subscribe` methods registered for its type.

entries.name: ApplicationEventPublisher
entries.detail: Components publish events through the context, which dispatches them to `@EventListener` methods; publishers never reference listeners.

entries.name: DispatcherServlet
entries.detail: Coordinates `HandlerMapping`, `HandlerAdapter` and `ViewResolver` collaborators, which never call each other directly.

entries.name: MediatR
entries.detail: Named for the pattern: `IMediator.Send` routes a request object to its single registered handler, so senders never reference handlers.

options.why: Peers communicate only through a central object that holds the coordination rule.
The tower decides what each plane does; it is not just broadcasting a change to passive listeners.
A facade is used one way by clients and unknown to the subsystem; here planes depend on the tower and call it.
The request is not passed from handler to handler; one object makes the decision.

exercises.scenario: A dialog has ten widgets whose enabled state, visibility and validation depend on each other. Each widget currently holds references to several others, and changing a rule means editing five classes.

options.why: Centralizes the many-to-many dependencies into one class so widgets stop referencing each other.
Each widget would still subscribe to several others, keeping the tangle and scattering the rules.
A facade offers a simpler outward API; it does not coordinate two-way interactions among peers.
The problem is coordination among objects, not swapping one algorithm.

exercises.prompt: Explain Mediator in your own words: what problem it solves, what it costs, and how it differs from Observer.

modelAnswer.text: Mediator replaces a tangle of direct references between peers with a central object that owns their interaction rules. Peers only know the mediator, so they become reusable. The cost is a mediator that can grow into a god class. Observer broadcasts changes one-to-many without coordination logic.

keyPoints: Peers talk through one object, not each other
Interaction rules live in the mediator
Risk: the mediator becomes a god class
